title: US Economic Resilience Comes From Consumers Borrowing From the Future
dek: Barkin unpacks why consumption stays strong despite high prices: consumers cut savings, fall behind on bills, and defer loan payments to keep spending; AI investment so far is more about price increases and crowding out than a productivity dividend; the Fed may face a long headwind.
why: Micro-level evidence a Fed official hears on the ground: consumers borrowing from the future to sustain spending, AI construction crowding out traditional building, tariff refunds stimulating earnings. Useful for calibrating judgments on US inflation stickiness and AI capex.
who: Investors, macro traders and Fed policy watchers who want to understand how US consumption resilience and AI investment affect the inflation and rate outlook.
skip: You can skip the last two minutes of show promotion and Mount Airy chit-chat; Barkin's main segment has no repeated content.

points.h: You can't extract forward guidance from someone who doesn't give it
points.body: Asked how he viewed Warsh's Jackson Hole remarks, Barkin said he listened carefully to the speech but explicitly refused to derive September FOMC action from it. "He personally doesn't like forward guidance, so you shouldn't look for forward guidance from someone who doesn't give forward guidance." Barkin stressed you can have a good discussion about the economy, but if the choice is not to give forward guidance, then you don't. The line was effectively also a response to the market's tendency to always try to extract a rate path from Fed officials' remarks. He described that impulse as "we can't help but want to know," but said it should be restrained.

points.h: Consumers' money is borrowed from the future
points.body: Barkin's observation: unlike the Great Recession, during the pandemic people accumulated a lot of cash, stocks and housing wealth, and formed a mindset of "I insist on spending." The key is that low-income consumers are also "creatively finding money": shifting to Walmart and dollar stores, cutting insurance, moving kids back home, not paying the gas bill in summer, letting auto loans go to 60 days rather than 120 days delinquent — in essence "borrowing from the future." His conclusion: as long as employment and asset markets are healthy, this spending sustained by lower savings and delinquent bills will continue. This micro mechanism explains the economy's "resilience" better than macro data.

points.h: Data centers pushed ordinary buildings out of the construction cycle
points.body: In one week early in the year, $700 billion of investment was announced; transformers, switchgear and electricians are all in short supply. Barkin thinks the construction cycle is shifting from offices and multifamily housing to data centers and industrial, and that multifamily housing "doesn't pencil out" can't be blamed on rates alone, because in 2004-05 rates were similarly high and buildings were still going up in volume. He acknowledges data center construction has indeed pushed up the cost of other construction, creating a "chicken-and-egg" crowding-out effect, but says it's hard to pin down exactly how much. The answer is a restrained display of the real disagreement inside the institution over the spillover effects of AI capex.

points.h: AI is hitting hiring first, not output
points.body: The AI questions Barkin hears at every chamber of commerce and town hall are political: jobs, water, data centers. Economically, AI's productivity shock is still concentrated in a few replaceable use cases like call centers, programming and clerical work; current productivity improvement comes more from the automation and process reengineering driven by the 2022 labor shortage. On the hiring side, employers are already using the logic of "can we let AI do it first, then decide whether to hire" to hold down hiring. Enthusiasm for AI is asymmetric between firms and workers: bosses are keen, employees are lukewarm. In other words, AI is currently affecting the economy by reducing labor demand rather than by raising output.

points.h: Choosing an inflation narrative is choosing a rate path
points.body: Barkin sums up today's inflation as two readings. One is "65 months without hitting target, don't give excuses," corresponding to Warsh's hawkish stance: inflation has been above target for a long time and rates may not be tight enough. The other is "47 months up plus 18 months down": post-pandemic inflation appeared, and after rate hikes it had fallen back to 2.3%-2.4% by March 2025, and it was the later AI, tariff and oil price shocks that pushed it back up. He explicitly says the second is "perfectly defensible," and "we will push it back down again later." Which narrative prevails determines whether the Fed keeps tightening or waits for the shocks to fade.

points.h: Tariffs are now stimulus, because the refunds have landed
points.body: The tariff topic is quieter than half a year ago, not because trade no longer matters, but because refunds landed after the Supreme Court ruling. Barkin says that over the past three or four months firms received refunds rather than paying extra tariffs. Steel and aluminum producers benefited by treating tariffs as a "price umbrella"; foreign manufacturers shipping European components to the US for assembly were instead hurt by the tariffs. The refunds are "very positive" for corporate earnings, and firms will use them for marketing, store renovations, and maintaining hiring, so there is a stimulus effect, but the pass-through to prices is "very targeted," not systemic. That explains why people aren't complaining much about tariffs right now.

points.h: The tax base data centers provide doesn't buy political acceptance
points.body: Local residents dislike data centers because, unlike factories, they don't have workers' kids playing ball with local kids, and the tax base benefits touted by economic developers lack political resonance. Barkin half-jokingly says you should name an elementary school after Microsoft or Google to win hearts and minds. He admits he doesn't know how large the data center buildout will be, and that the AI footprint, data center footprint and energy demand could all be substantially underestimated or overestimated. If political backlash leads to underbuilding, it will drag on growth; if there's overbuilding, it will worsen inflation. This is an uncertainty not yet incorporated into the policy framework.

points.h: AI could be inflationary or deflationary, so don't bet in advance
points.body: On whether AI brings a productivity boom and lifts the neutral rate R-star, Barkin is cautious. He says the AI path one, two, three years out has an "extremely wide range," and could show up as either inflation or deflation, with 18 versions in between. Until he has enough confidence, policy can't be set on assumptions. He also responded to Warsh's view: different AI models point to completely opposite rate directions. So he implies the Fed should wait for data rather than putting AI productivity into the dot plot in advance. That statement is a warning to those betting on a higher R-star.

quotes.text: And I'm not saying inflation is definitely heading in the wrong direction. It's just not in the right place.
So people are finding ways to effectively borrow from the future, savings rates down.
I don't think it's ridiculous to imagine that 10 years later you might have a bunch of factors that would bring inflation up.
And if what's happening is that picture is swamping the narrative, then we're going to think differently about the picture.
Well, I'm definitely 100% insistent on getting inflation under control.
Those big box retailers, they're truly our strongest soldiers in the fight against inflation, holding the line on prices on behalf of the customer.
I think the anecdote doesn't, everyone likes a good story, but it doesn't really move policy.
